name: Americanism
summary: Americanism is loyalty to the United States and to the political creed its defining sources see as its founding principles. In its best-known form, the 'one hundred percent Americanism' of Theodore Roosevelt and the Americanization movement, it demands undivided national allegiance, the English language and the assimilation of immigrants, judges citizens by conduct rather than ancestry or creed, and keeps church and state apart. A second strand, set out by C. Bradley Thompson with Ayn Rand's and Leonard Read's texts, reads it as the individual-rights philosophy of the Declaration of Independence: limited government, private property and free exchange. The word is famously contested, and its sources divide wherever these strands, or the later left and right uses Thompson reports, disagree.
scope: As the defining sources set it out: the Encyclopedia of European Social History entry (s7) treats Americanism as the American equivalent of nationalism, the post-1918 'one hundred percent Americanism' movement, and in another sense the central tenets of the American creed; Olneck (s8) describes the creedal American identity and the World War I campaigns for 100 Percent Americanism; Dorsey (s9) ties Roosevelt's speeches and essays to his Americanism; Thompson (s6) defines it as the Declaration's individual-rights philosophy, names Rand's Textbook of Americanism and Read's 'The Essence of Americanism' as its classic statements, and reports that the Left now identifies it with multiculturalism, regulation and welfarism and the Right with Christianity, school prayer, tradition, family values and community standards. The profile answers from these sources and the texts they tie to the term: Roosevelt's 'True Americanism' (1894) and 'Americanism' (1915), the American Legion's preamble ('one hundred percent Americanism') and its magazine's account of that Americanism, Rand's Textbook and Read's speech. Where these strands, or the uses Thompson documents, take opposite sides it is a split (0, low). Catholic 'Americanism' (the heresy condemned in 1899), nativist and Klan claims to the word, and the Communist Party's slogan are outside the profile, as are the broader subjects American nationalism, exceptionalism and civil religion. Kazin and McCartin's Americanism (2006), Gelernter's Americanism (2007) and Wall's Inventing the 'American Way' could not be read in an open copy.

sources.author: Theodore Roosevelt (excerpts, Teaching American History)
sources.usedFor: Americanism as spirit, not creed or birthplace; national rather than sectional; Americanizing immigrants in speech, political ideas and church-state relations; English-only public schools; no division of the school fund; no ethnic or religious voting; drastic immigration restriction including races that do not assimilate readily.

sources.title: Textbook of Americanism (The Vigil, 1946)
sources.author: Ayn Rand (FEE's PDF of the copy Rand delivered to Leonard Read)
sources.usedFor: Named by Thompson (s6) as a classic statement of Americanism. sources.author: Leonard E. Read, Foundation for Economic Education
sources.usedFor: Named by Thompson (s6) as a statement of Americanism. notes: Rules-5 pass by claude-opus-5-5 (2026-11-08), brought up to the shared rules because the page gets search traffic. The first pass (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-10-16) answered largely from Wikipedia's Americanism and American exceptionalism articles and from the Gettysburg Address, and recorded positions it judged adherents split on as 0. Under rules 5 Wikipedia is not evidence and the Gettysburg Address is not tied to Americanism by any defining source, so every first-pass answer was re-answered from the sources below or nulled, with the first version kept in its reviewHistory (s1, s4 and s5 stay listed for that history). This pass read in full Thompson's essay, the two Gale encyclopedia entries, Roosevelt's 1915 address and the 1894 excerpts, the Legion preamble and magazine account, Rand's Textbook (OCR of FEE's scan) and Read's speech. Themes searched: economy (property, welfare, taxes, trade, planning, inflation), government (democracy, Constitution, rights, majority rule), society and culture (religion, language, assimilation, race, education), liberty (force, self-ownership, censorship) and world (defence, conscription, loyalty, foreign influence). The defining sources say little on ecology, technology, alliances, the UN or social questions such as abortion and drugs, and Thompson's report that Left and Right attach opposite values to the word turns several society and economy statements into splits. Not read: Kazin and McCartin, Americanism: New Perspectives on the History of an Ideal (UNC Press 2006; no open copy, Everand preview only), Gelernter (2007), Wall (2008), the 1915 American Journal of Sociology symposium 'What is Americanism?' (a survey of 250 opinions, not a definition).
